tldr: Guided by the linguistic framework FrameNet, HiPHI is an ultra-large-scale dataset for humanoid reinforcement learning that systematically covers human motion space, providing 617.5 hours of sub-millimeter precision optical motion capture with synchronized object meshes.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline constructing the HiPHI motion space from the linguistic framework FrameNet. Motion seeds are selected as robotic-relevant events (Frames) and lexical units (LUs) such as verbs, which are then systematically combined with variations in speed, direction, and contact conditions to build a vast, unbiased motion manifold.
overview:
Teaching humanoid robots general-purpose whole-body locomotion and object manipulation requires massive amounts of reference motion data. However, data collection has long faced a major dilemma. Real-robot teleoperation is costly and difficult to scale, while web video data only provides visual information lacking precise physical contacts and joint states. Furthermore, conventional motion capture (MoCap) data mostly relies on manually scripted scenarios tailored for animation, suffering from limited coverage and a lack of accurate physical interactions with objects. For instance, data showing an 'invisible chair' sit without an actual chair prevents a robot from learning physically grounded, stable control.

To address this, the authors drew inspiration from how WordNet structured ImageNet for computer vision. They devised a methodology to systematically design motion space using FrameNet, a linguistic framework of frame semantics, as a conceptual scaffold. By extracting robotic-relevant event frames and lexical units (LUs) as seeds, they systematically crossed them with physical parameters—such as speed, direction, amplitude, load, and contact conditions—to generate comprehensive motion scenarios.

Following this design, they recorded the HiPHI dataset using high-precision optical MoCap across 132 human actors, totaling 617.5 hours (including 245.7 hours of object interactions). 3D object meshes and 6-DoF trajectories are fully synchronized at sub-millimeter accuracy.

Experiments evaluated motion-space coverage using unsupervised kinematic embeddings, physical quality such as joint jerk, floor penetration, and object collision, as well as whole-body tracking reinforcement learning and real-world deployment on the Unitree G1 robot. HiPHI significantly outperforms existing datasets in diversity and physical consistency, and policies trained on it stably perform diverse behaviors—including running, sitting, box carrying, and suitcase pulling—on the real hardware.
contributions: Established a motion collection pipeline anchored in the linguistic framework FrameNet to theoretically and systematically cover and expand the motion space required for humanoids.

Constructed 617.5 total hours (including mirrored data) of sub-millimeter precision optical MoCap, featuring 245.7 hours of object-contact interactions with synchronized 3D meshes and 6-DoF trajectories.

Provided a comprehensive benchmark suite evaluating motion-space coverage, geometric and physical consistency with floors and objects, and motion-tracking performance in both physical simulation and real-world humanoid deployment.

sections.heading: Bridging the Gap: Scale and Physical Precision in Humanoid Learning
sections.summary: Humanoid policy learning demands data with diverse whole-body motions and accurately grounded physical object interactions. Grounded in the linguistic resource FrameNet, this work systematizes motion space and presents HiPHI, an ultra-large-scale dataset captured via high-precision optical MoCap.
sections.details:
To operate in the physical world, humanoid robots must learn dynamic balance, postural transitions, inter-limb coordination, and control strategies responsive to contact and payload.

Yet, existing data sources suffer from critical trade-offs. Real-robot teleoperation data is extremely expensive to collect and hardware-specific. Internet videos and egocentric footage offer diversity but cannot directly provide joint angles or contact states, suffering from estimation noise. Meanwhile, conventional MoCap collected for CG animation and human understanding features narrow behavioral coverage and lacks accurately synchronized object contacts.

This work reframes data collection as a 'motion-space design problem'. By leveraging the semantically structured FrameNet to define motion seeds, scenarios are systematically generated across modulation factors such as direction, velocity, and load.

Captured from 132 actors, HiPHI spans 617.5 hours (with bilateral mirroring), including 245.7 hours of object manipulation. Because 3D object meshes and poses are simultaneously tracked, the dataset serves as physically executable reference motions for robots.

sections.heading: How HiPHI Differs from Teleoperation, Video, and Prior MoCap
sections.summary: By reviewing the limitations of teleoperation, video-based datasets, conventional human MoCap, and human-object interaction (HOI) datasets, the authors position HiPHI as the first large-scale foundation combining vast scale, high precision, systematic coverage, and synchronized object tracking.
sections.details:
This section categorizes data sources in robotics and embodied AI into three main streams:

- Robot Teleoperation and Egocentric Data: Approaches like UMI and teleoperation eliminate the embodiment gap, but they incur high collection costs and are tied to specific robot hardware. Egocentric video covers diverse everyday tasks, but cannot directly measure forces, contacts, or precise 3D body poses.
- Human Motion Capture (MoCap) Data: Datasets such as AMASS, LAFAN1, HumanML3D, and BONES-SEED are widely used in animation and CG synthesis, but their coverage is ad-hoc rather than systematically constructed for robotic control.
- Human-Object Interaction (HOI) Data: While object-centric MoCap datasets like OMOMO and HIMO have emerged, they remain limited in scale (a few to tens of hours) and lack physical contact precision and behavioral variety.

HiPHI resolves these challenges at once, standing out through its large scale, sub-millimeter optical precision, FrameNet-guided systematic design, and synchronized object data.

sections.heading: Beyond Ad-Hoc Scripting: Systematizing Motion Space with FrameNet
sections.summary: Instead of haphazardly capturing daily routines, FrameNet semantic frames and Lexical Units (LUs) were adopted to target control-relevant behaviors. Applying physical and geometric modulations to each LU seed enables a systematic, extensible motion-space construction.
sections.details:
What humanoids need is not a direct recording of a typical human day. Over-indexing on behaviors like 'watching TV' is useless for a robot; control-critical patterns like locomotion, postural transitions, dynamic balance, and responses to external constraints are essential.

Traditionally, designers manually scripted daily activities. This often causes redundant motions with different contexts (e.g., 'wiping sweat' vs. 'shading eyes' share the exact same kinematics). Conversely, a simple behavior like 'walking' yields entirely different dynamics when changing speed, turning direction, or stride length. Accumulating handwritten scripts makes it impossible to know which areas of the motion manifold are covered or missing.

HiPHI addresses this by adopting an approach analogous to ImageNet's use of WordNet. Using FrameNet, it defines semantic 'Frames' and context-specific 'Lexical Units' (LUs). For instance, 'walk' and 'run' under the Self_motion frame are selected as seeds.

Common Augment Factors are then systematically applied to each seed to instruct performers:
- Path and direction (straight, circular, shuttle runs, etc.)
- Speed and rhythm (slow, fast, sudden stops, etc.)
- Amplitude and posture (wide strides, crouching, upper/lower body involvement)
- Object and contact conditions (object type, weight, pushing, pulling, carrying, etc.)

To prevent artifacts like 'invisible chair' sitting where no support object is tracked, interacting objects are tracked simultaneously. This guarantees fully grounded physical interaction data.

captions.F3: Comparison between conventional manual scripting and HiPHI's FrameNet-guided pipeline. While traditional methods add ad-hoc tasks resulting in unclear coverage (left), HiPHI systematically expands seeds using shared augment factors, scaling motion-space coverage in a principled manner (right).

sections.heading: Over 600 Hours: Massive Scale and Rich Metadata
sections.summary: Recorded from 132 actors at 90Hz, HiPHI totals 617.5 hours (approx. 200M frames) including bilateral mirroring. It covers both frequent primitives and an extensive long tail of atypical behaviors, complete with 40 real-world interaction objects.
sections.details:
Specific composition and statistics of HiPHI are as follows:

- Scale and Tracking Precision: Captured from 132 human subjects (76 males, 56 females, 155–185 cm, 40–82 kg) at 90Hz using an optical MoCap system. Following standards like BONES-SEED, applying bilateral mirroring brings the total duration to 617.5 hours (308.7 hours raw), comprising roughly 200 million frames.
- Motion Breakdown: 371.8 hours of body-only motion and 245.7 hours of human-object interaction (HOI). Motions are categorized into 22 frames and 214 Frame-LUs, with each clip annotated with Frame-LU labels and natural language descriptions.
- Long-Tail Coverage: While the top 50 Frame-LUs account for 53.7% of the dataset, the remaining 46.3% forms a rich long tail of dynamic, irregular motions. An average of 24 distinct actors performed each LU, introducing strong intra-class diversity.
- Object Manipulation Suite: 40 real-world objects across 12 categories (furniture, containers, cleaning tools, sports equipment, etc., weighing 0.45–6.25 kg) are used to record interactions across 90 Frame-LUs (pushing, pulling, carrying, sitting, leaning, etc.). 3D object meshes and synchronized 6-DoF trajectories are provided.

captions.F4: Frame-LU composition and long-tail distribution in HiPHI: (a) duration proportion per frame, (b) distribution across LUs, and (c) cumulative coverage curve, demonstrating strong coverage of core motor primitives alongside a substantial long tail (approx. 46%) of uncommon behaviors.

sections.heading: Validated: Motion Coverage, Physical Fidelity, and Real-Robot Transfer
sections.summary: Evaluations of motion-space coverage, physical data quality (joint jerk, floor/object contacts), and reinforcement learning tracking on the Unitree G1 robot across simulation and hardware demonstrate decisive advantages over existing datasets.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted along two primary axes: intrinsic dataset properties and downstream humanoid learning performance.

5.1 Motion-Space Diversity
An unsupervised temporal convolutional autoencoder was trained on uniformly sampled motion windows across datasets, and the 16D latent space was projected to 2D via t-SNE. Under a $55\times 55$ grid partition, HiPHI occupied 1,620 cells, substantially exceeding the closest strong baseline BONES-SEED (1,438 cells). HiPHI also led in entropy-based effective cell count (1,443 vs. 1,114) and long-tail proportion (14.1% vs. 10.7%), proving it expands uniformly into uncharted motion regions rather than merely over-sampling common primitives.

5.2 Data Quality
- Smoothness and Grounding: Measured metrics included joint jerk $\mathcal{J}_{\tau}$, acceleration $\mathcal{A}$, floor penetration $\delta_{\text{ground}}$, floating ratio $\phi_{\text{float}}$, and foot sliding velocity $\nu_{\text{foot}}$. HiPHI achieved the best scores across all metrics among datasets sharing a unified floor plane.
- Object Contact Consistency: HiPHI achieved a non-collision rate $\eta_{\text{nc}}$ of 98.1% (preventing mesh penetration) and a near-surface contact rate $\rho_{\text{near}}$ of 95.7%, substantially outperforming prior HOI datasets OMOMO (50.4%) and HIMO (79.0%).

5.3 Humanoid Learning
A DeepMimic-style RL pipeline trained whole-body tracking policies on the Unitree G1 robot. Comparing against LAFAN1, AMASS, BONES-SEED, and Motion-X++ under identical data budgets (3 and 20 hours), HiPHI demonstrated the highest tracking success and fastest convergence. Furthermore, scaling HiPHI training data from 3 to 300 hours consistently reduced generalization tracking error (MPJPE) on unseen datasets. For object manipulation (kicking, carrying, pushing, leaning), HiPHI achieved the lowest tracking errors for both robot and object.

5.4 Real-World Evaluation
Trained policies were deployed zero-shot (Sim-to-Real) on the physical Unitree G1. The robot stably performed dynamic and contact-rich whole-body tasks without failure, including running, sitting on a chair, crawling on all fours, carrying a box, rolling on the ground, and pulling a wheeled suitcase.

captions.F5: Motion-space visualization via a shared autoencoder: (a) global latent projection, (b) support region comparison against the strongest baseline BONES-SEED, and (c) occupied grid statistics. HiPHI's boundary largely encompasses BONES-SEED, covering the space more extensively and uniformly.
captions.F6: Whole-body imitation tracking performance on Unitree G1: (a) tracking success rates under matched 3-hour and 20-hour data budgets, and (b) failure rate progression during training. HiPHI learns the fastest and achieves a distinctly lower final failure rate.
captions.F8: Real-world humanoid deployment (Unitree G1) using policies trained on HiPHI: (a) running, (b) sitting, (c) crawling, (d) box carrying, (e) rolling over, and (f) suitcase pulling, successfully demonstrating contact-rich dynamic behaviors on physical hardware.

sections.heading: Summary: A Next-Generation Benchmark for Embodied Intelligence
sections.summary: By designing motion space through FrameNet, HiPHI establishes an ultra-large-scale, high-precision, object-synchronized motion benchmark. Extensive experiments confirm it provides a scalable data foundation for real-world humanoid whole-body control and object manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper presented HiPHI, a 617.5-hour high-precision optical MoCap dataset aimed at advancing humanoid intelligence.

The FrameNet-guided seed augmentation pipeline theoretically and systematically maximizes motion-space coverage. Moreover, 245.7 hours of interactions with synchronized 3D object meshes and trajectories elevate physical fidelity in contact-rich settings.

Across coverage, physical quality, simulation tracking, and real-world deployment, HiPHI overcomes the limitations of existing datasets and establishes a scalable learning foundation for humanoid control policies.

sections.heading: Current Limitations and Future Directions
sections.summary: Key constraints include the restriction to single-actor motions, the absence of direct contact force and tactile measurements, and capture within an optical studio rather than in-the-wild environments.
sections.details:
The authors identify three main limitations of HiPHI:

- Single-Actor Scenarios: Currently, HiPHI only captures single-person motions, excluding multi-person collaboration or physical human-human interactions.
- Kinematics-Centric Data: While high-precision joint trajectories and 6-DoF object poses are recorded, contact force vectors and tactile signals at the feet and hands are not directly measured.
- Studio Capture: Because recordings took place in a controlled optical MoCap studio, extending coverage to diverse in-the-wild daily environments (such as egocentric camera captures) remains an open challenge for future work.

takeaways: Shifting motion data collection from ad-hoc script guessing to a systematic design—linguistic seeds via FrameNet combined with physical modulations—is highly principled and scalable.

In humanoid learning, physical consistency (minimizing foot sliding, ground penetration, and mesh collision) is just as critical as total dataset duration for policy learning and sim-to-real transfer.
Providing millimeter-accurate synchronized 6-DoF trajectories and 3D meshes for objects (chairs, boxes, etc.) enables direct training of whole-body manipulation skills like reaching and carrying.
limitations: Contact force vectors from force plates or tactile sensors are not directly measured; dynamic parameters still depend on simulation or estimation.
Being recorded in an optical MoCap studio, the dataset lacks the sensory and visual diversity found in egocentric, in-the-wild captures with real-world obstacles.
Multi-person interactions (assisting, collaborative carrying, close physical interaction) are not included.
